headline: The Brain Uploads Itself (and Other Afternoon Ideas)
subheadline: Whole-brain emulation meets open-hardware skulls — the first two transcripts out of the harvest fleet, and the sandbox is already arguing with philosophers
theme: d/acc, identity, and the red pill
themeSub: written from the first 2 of 40 transcripts — the dispatch grows as the fleet delivers
stats: Philosophers invoked: Locke, Hume, Nietzsche, Dennett, Parfit

body.content: The harvest fleet delivered its first two transcripts from the alpine cold, and what an opening pair: one builder proposing to emulate a whole mouse brain — and asking which philosophers survive the procedure — and another strapping open-source hardware to human skulls because the alternative is renting your own biometrics back from a platform.
🧠 Where am I? (Asking for a brain in a vat)

Christian, co-founder of a whole-brain emulation startup with two animal labs in the UK, opened the d/acc afternoon by doing something rare in tech: taking identity seriously before shipping. His premise — every conversation about brain emulation hits the same local minimum, where you must decide what you think a self even is. Ego theory, psychological continuity, materialism, the no-self view. He toured the canon, then gently noted that the canon hasn't updated itself for neuroscience — split-brain patients whose two hemispheres disagree, one hand reaching for the coffee while the other holds it back; the life-stories we spin about ourselves that our lived experience quietly contradicts.

body.text: Identity is the conditions that underlie the existence of a system.
body.speaker: Christian, on the formalists

body.content: His favorite thought experiment is Dennett's «Where Am I?» — a NASA mission, a nuclear warhead in a Houston ravine, and a brain named Yorick placed in a vat while its body, Fortinbras, goes to work by radio link. The question that has launched a thousand philosophy seminar fights: where is the real I? And then, the pivot that made the room sit up: Puja Ohlhaver's soulbound tokens, invoked earlier that day, as a way identity might one day be quantified — a bridge between the metaphysics and the Merkle trees.
💊 The red pill, manufactured in Amsterdam

The second transcript is smaller and scrappier and perfect: an intro to brain-computer interfaces from the Think2Earn camp, who build open-hardware fNIRS headsets — near-infrared spectroscopy you can manufacture yourself — because one in eight people on Earth carries a mental or neurological disorder, a quarter of healthcare spending in the developed world goes to meeting it — and the choice, as they frame it, is a pill of a particular color.

body.text: Would you choose red pill — open hardware, brain-computer interfaces, open source software — or would you want to wait for the big companies to make their proprietary tech and extract as much value as possible from your biometrics?
body.speaker: the Think2Earn builder
body.session: An Intro to BCIs, Open Hardware, and the think2earn Model

body.content: Between the two talks a thesis assembles itself, the way d/acc afternoons do: if minds might someday run on new substrates, then who owns the electrodes matters enormously. Upload the brain or defend it — either way, you'll want the hardware to be open.
